claims.claim: Well diggers struck a ten-foot stone man (the Cardiff Giant was about ten feet long and found by men digging a well)
claims.quote: It was a 10-foot-tall (3.0 m), roughly 3,000 pound purported "petrified man", uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York.

claims.claim: The giant photograph is by Bain News Service, 1910, public domain
claims.quote:
Date: 1910
Author: Bain News Service, publisher
Licence: Public domain

claims.claim: The print lists the figure as 10 feet 4½ inches long with a nose of 6 inches
claims.quote: Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches; from crown of head to chin, 1 foot, 9 inches; length of nose, 6 inches

claims.claim: George Hull had the giant carved in his own likeness
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: The lithograph is titled "The Onondaga Giant" and is from Popular Graphic Arts
claims.quote: Archive title: File:The Onondaga giant LCCN2003666806.jpg ... Author: Popular Graphic Arts

claims.claim: The giant began as a block of gypsum
claims.quote: Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The block was quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, in 1868
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The workmen were told the stone was intended for a Lincoln monument
claims.quote: telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: The stereocard image shows the Fort Dodge gypsum quarry, "View in Cardiff Glen," 1873
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: The stereocard verso names George Hull and H. B. Martin as the perpetrators
claims.quote: The perpetrators of the imposture are well remembered by old residents of Fort Dodge. Their names were George Hull and H. B. Martin.

claims.claim: Whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what he was carving is not clear
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving

claims.claim: On 16 October 1869 two men digging a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, found the stone body
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: Newell put a tent over the giant
claims.quote: He covered the giant with a tent and it soon became an attraction site.

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing
claims.quote: a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people a day came
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day as the demand for wagons and carriages dramatically increased.

claims.claim: The giant belonged to Newell's cousin, George Hull
claims.quote: During November 1868, Hull transported the giant by railroad to the farm of his cousin, William Newell.

claims.claim: George Hull was a tobacconist
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: Hull had lost an argument at a revival meeting about the giants named in Genesis 6:4
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: Hull shipped the block to a stonecutter in Chicago
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: A geologist told Hull hair does not petrify, so the giant is beardless
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: Sand and water, sulphuric acid, and a board of steel knitting needles were used to age the surface
claims.quote: Hull first wiped the giant using a sponge soaked with sand and water. The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores. The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: The hoax cost $2,600
claims.quote: By then, he had spent US$2,600 (equivalent to $63,000 in 2025) for the hoax.

claims.claim: Geologists saw through the hoax quickly
claims.quote: John F. Boynton, the first geologist to examine the giant, declared that it could not be a fossilized man

claims.claim: Yale's O. C. Marsh called the giant "a most decided humbug"
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue ... and termed it "a most decided humbug".

claims.claim: Marsh noted the statue was soluble gypsum still carrying fresh tool marks
claims.quote: pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did)

claims.claim: Andrew D. White questioned why a well would be dug there when a good spring already ran conveniently to the house
claims.quote: there was no reason why the farmer should dig a well in the spot where the figure was found; that it was convenient neither to the house nor to the barn; that there was already a good spring and a stream of water running conveniently to both

claims.claim: Hull confessed on 10 December 1869
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: In February 1870 a court declared both giants fake
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: Barnum made a plaster copy after his $50,000 offer for the giant was refused
claims.quote: showman P. T. Barnum offered $50,000 for the giant. When the syndicate refused, he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy.

claims.claim: The Chicago stonecutter's name was Edward Burkhardt
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.
